The same rule applies to the feminine form. Before a feminine singular noun that begins with a stressed "a" sound, buena shortens to buen. For instance, "un buen año" means "a good year," and "un buen agua" would mean "good water," though in practice you'd more likely say "un agua buena." This shortening occurs because the masculine buen and feminine buena share the same form before vowels to avoid awkward sound combinations.

Other Spanish adjectives follow this same pattern. Malo becomes mal before masculine singular nouns, as in "mal día" or "bad day." Grande becomes gran before both masculine and feminine singular nouns, so you say "gran hombre" or "gran mujer" rather than "grande hombre." The prosgegrammeni, literally "added to the letter," refers to the iota subscript that appears beneath certain vowels in Greek text—a feature inherited from ancient Greek polytonic writing. The ypogegrammeni, meaning "written beneath," similarly describes the iota adscript that historically accompanied long vowels in Greek, though in modern Greek usage these marks have largely fallen out of common practice. In the medieval period, these spellings were replaced by spellings with an iota subscript, to mark former diphthongs which were no longer pronounced.
